title: Snooker was invented in India
hook: Snooker is usually traced to bored army officers in central India in 1875.
peek: The game played in smoky British halls began in an officers' mess in Jabalpur, India. Its name came from army slang for a raw first-year cadet, thrown at a player who missed an easy shot.
lede: In 1875 British army officers in Jabalpur, in central India, were playing billiards variants through the rainy season. The usual story credits Neville Chamberlain, a young officer, with adding coloured balls to a game called black pool. When a fellow officer missed a pot, Chamberlain called him a snooker, slang for a first-year cadet. The name stuck to the game.

bullets.text: At the Royal Military Academy in Woolwich, new cadets were nicknamed snookers. Chamberlain later explained that he applied the word to a beginner's miss, and players took it as a name for the game.

The officer was Sir Neville Francis Fitzgerald Chamberlain, a soldier and later a police chief in Ireland, not the prime minister of the same name. He set out its origin in a 1938 letter to The Field magazine.
Chamberlain moved to Ootacamund, now Ooty, where the Ooty Club still claims the game's rules were settled. Much of the history rests on Chamberlain's own account.
Snooker spread through officers returning home. It turned professional in Britain, and in 1927 Joe Davis won the first world championship.
